analysis.one_liner: Protects patients from surprise out-of-network medical bills by charging them in-network prices.
analysis.headline: The House Ways and Means Committee approved it on a voice vote in February 2020, but the full House never voted on it before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: When you go to the emergency room or a hospital in your insurance network, you can still get hit with huge bills from doctors there who are outside your network. This bill would stop that: patients would pay only their normal in-network copays and deductibles, insurance companies would pay out-of-network doctors a set rate based on the middle of what similar doctors charge, and both sides could dispute the amount in a mediation process. It also adds price-estimate, provider-directory, and air-ambulance reporting rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with private health insurance who might need emergency care, surgery, childbirth, or other hospital treatment. Today, a person can do everything right — go to an in-network hospital — and still be billed thousands of dollars by an out-of-network anesthesiologist, radiologist, or emergency physician they had no say in choosing. The bill makes the patient responsible only for what an in-network doctor would have cost, and it forbids the provider from billing the patient for the rest.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Privately insured patients getting emergency or hospital care

how_it_helps.text: Patients who receive emergency services, or covered care from an out-of-network provider at an in-network hospital, would pay no more than the in-network cost-sharing amount, calculated using the plan's median in-network rate [S2][S3].

Providers would be prohibited from balance billing — chasing the patient for the difference between their charge and what the plan pays — for emergency services and for services furnished by a nonparticipating provider at a participating facility, in specified cases [S2][S3].

In states without their own dispute process, plans and out-of-network providers would settle payment through open negotiation and, if that fails, a mediated dispute before an independent entity [S2][S3].

The bill adds practical help beyond the billing fight: public provider directories, cost estimates for services scheduled at least three days out, coverage protections for patients whose plan's contract with a long-term-care facility ends, plan-card information and price-comparison tools, and direct access to OB-GYN and pediatric providers without a referral [S2][S3].
A temporary tax deduction would let people deduct surprise-billing and emergency out-of-network expenses that otherwise fall below the 7.5%-of-income floor [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Out-of-network doctors and the companies that staff emergency rooms, anesthesiology, radiology and other specialties — including private-equity-backed staffing firms — would be paid a benchmarked amount (the median in-network contracted rate) rather than their full billed charges, and could no longer bill patients for the difference. Insurers take on new compliance, directory, audit, and cost-estimate duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Out-of-network physicians, staffing firms, and insurers

drawbacks.text: Setting out-of-network payment at the median in-network contracted rate gives insurers strong leverage in contract talks; doctors' groups argued this approach lets insurers set below-market rates, which over time could push some physicians out of networks or raise premiums [S2].

The temporary deduction for surprise-billing expenses costs the Treasury revenue and helps most those with large enough out-of-pocket bills to itemize beyond the income floor, which is only partial relief for the people the bill is meant to protect [S2][S3].
The advance cost-estimate requirement applies only to services scheduled at least three days ahead, so it does nothing for emergency patients, the group most exposed to surprise bills [S2][S3].

Compliance duties for insurers — provider directories, price-comparison tools, member-card information, and government audits of their rate calculations — add administrative cost that insurers may pass to customers through premiums [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the upside is large and direct: it removes one of the most common ways a medical emergency turns into crushing debt, and it does not change what care you can get. The costs fall mostly on providers who built revenue on high out-of-network charges and on insurers facing new paperwork. The bill's design leans toward insurers by pegging payment to a median-rate benchmark, and its tax deduction is an imperfect patch. On balance it is a genuine consumer protection whose costs land on concentrated interests rather than on patients.

outcome.mechanism: The House Ways and Means Committee ordered it reported, amended, on a voice vote in February 2020, but the House leadership never brought it to the floor before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 10, 2020, by Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA), chairman of the Ways and Means Committee, and referred to four committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, and Transportation and Infrastructure [S1][S5].
It drew 40 cosponsors, 22 House Republicans and 18 House Democrats — a bipartisan roster for a consumer billing bill [S4].
Two days after introduction, on February 12, 2020, the Ways and Means Committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported in the nature of a substitute (amended) by voice vote [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the bill was never reported to the House floor, never debated, and never voted on, and it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Out-of-network physicians and physician-staffing firms, whose revenues depend on out-of-network charges, avoided the median-rate payment benchmark while the bill sat unscheduled. Patients did get surprise-billing protections that same winter, when Congress passed a different surprise-billing law as part of the year-end government funding package in December 2020.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Out-of-network providers and staffing firms, for now

for.name: Rep. Richard E. Neal
for.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought it through his committee, which ordered it reported, amended, on a voice vote two days after introduction.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote in the ten months after the Ways and Means Committee ordered it reported.

against.name: American Medical Association and organized physicians
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the benchmark-based approach to setting out-of-network payment, arguing it hands insurers too much power to set rates; several physician and staffing-industry-backed groups pushed for the rival arbitration-based approach.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split 22 Republicans and 18 Democrats, and the Ways and Means Committee advanced it on a voice vote — the bill's problem was never partisan opposition in committee but the absence of a floor vote.

industries.note: These providers — including private-equity-backed firms staffing emergency rooms and anesthesia, radiology, and pathology groups — earn much of their revenue by charging out-of-network rates and billing patients for the balance. The bill pegs their payment to the median in-network rate and bans balance billing, directly cutting into that revenue model while saving patients from the resulting bills.

Insurers would pay out-of-network providers a median-rate benchmark instead of uncontrolled out-of-network charges, and would gain leverage in future contract negotiations. The same benchmark that cuts their payouts is what shields patients, so the industry's gain and the public's protection come from the same mechanism.

In-network hospitals lose the ability to let out-of-network specialists generate high patient bills, but the bill also directs plan payments to facilities rather than to patients in covered cases and shields hospitals' patients from disputes; hospitals were split on surprise-billing fixes generally.
The bill imposes new reporting requirements on air ambulance services, an industry known for very high out-of-network charges, but stops short of capping what they can bill in this bill's provisions.
The temporary deduction for surprise-billing expenses reduces federal revenue, a broad but small cost spread across all taxpayers.
